# Your Game Lab {#sec-game-lab}

## Remix with the three-step guide

Use **Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior** for every Game Lab experiment. Inspect the existing project first and keep any stage that already supports your change.

| Step | Where to look | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build the scene structure | Project `index.html`, scene setup in `main.js`, and any level data such as Robot Orchard’s `level.json`. | Required controls, objects, starting positions, and state exist. |
| Style the scene | Linked styles in `games/shared/`, canvas drawing, sprite assets, or 3D materials and lights. | The player can distinguish the changed object and understand its feedback. |
| Program game behavior | Input handlers, update functions, collision helpers, and game rules. | The change behaves as predicted during play, at boundaries, and after restart. |

For example, a new collectible needs a place and a stored collected state; a recognizable appearance; and a collection rule that updates the score only once. Add and test one collectible before making a whole new level. A color-only exercise can reuse the existing scene and rules, then check that the new color remains readable during play.

## Which games need a local web server?

::: {.callout-important title="Chapters 15–22: local HTTP server required" icon="false"}

**All six Game Lab projects require a web server.** Start the included launcher, then open the game through `http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/`. Double-clicking the game's `index.html` is not enough. Install Node.js once using the steps below; after that, double-click the launcher each time you play.

:::

| Game or example | Chapters | Local HTTP server? | Internet while playing? | Why? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure, Style, and Behavior scene examples; Monster Clicker; Catch the Star; Bouncing Ball; Pong; Breakout; Snake; your one-file Game Studio project | 2–14 | **No** for the supplied one-file examples | No | The game code is in the HTML file. Open that file in a browser. Keep any supplied images beside it. |
| Collision Playground | 15–16 | **Required** | No | Imports shared JavaScript modules. |
| Robot Orchard, including its sprite and level examples | 15–18 | **Required** | No | Imports modules and requests `level.json` and local artwork. |
| Robot Island Explorer | 19–20 | **Required** | **Yes, by default** | Imports Three.js and loads local GLB models. |
| 3D Asset Workshop | 20 | **Required** | **Yes, by default** | Imports Three.js and its addons, and loads a local GLB model. |
| Rapier Drop Lab | 21 | **Required** | **Yes, by default** | Imports Three.js and Rapier, then initializes physics. |
| Marble Quest | 22 | **Required** | **Yes, by default** | Imports Three.js and Rapier, and loads local models and textures. |

The six projects' extra demonstration and screenshot pages also use modules and require HTTP. The older one-file games in `workspace/` (including Secret Number, Treasure Clicker, and Rock–Paper–Scissors) can open directly. If you later add module imports or `fetch()` to a one-file game, use a server for that version too.

**Local HTTP and internet access are separate requirements.** The two 2D projects run offline after Node.js is installed. The four 3D projects need internet for their CDN libraries unless an adult has completed the optional offline setup later in this guide. They still need a local server after that setup. If the book and games are already on a working hosted website, open that site's game links; its web server supplies the files, so you do not need Node.js just to play online.

## Start a local server

The first one-file games can open directly from your drive. The Game Lab projects are different: their HTML pages load JavaScript modules, shared code, artwork, level data, or 3D models. A local web server gives the browser a safe way to ask for those files.

| How you open a page | Address you may see | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Double-click an HTML file | `file:///...` | A simple, complete one-file game. |
| Start a local server, then open its address | `http://127.0.0.1:8000/...` | This book's multi-file Game Lab projects. |

A server is not automatically a giant computer far away. Here it is a small program running on **your** computer. `127.0.0.1` is a special address that means “this computer.” It does not publish your work on the internet.

### One-time setup: install Node.js

The Game Lab's server is included in this textbook. It uses **Node.js**, a free program that can run JavaScript outside the browser. You do **not** need to install `npm` packages or find another web-server app.

Because installing software can require a password or school permission, do this step with a parent, teacher, or other adult:

Use the official download page: **[https://nodejs.org/en/download](https://nodejs.org/en/download)**. Choose the version marked **LTS** (long-term support). Use the installer download; you can skip the command-line installation instructions on that page. The version number changes over time.

#### Windows: install once

1. Open the download page above and select **Windows** and **LTS**.
2. Download the **Windows Installer (.msi)**. Choose **x64** for most Intel/AMD computers, or **ARM64** if **Settings → System → About → System type** says ARM-based processor.
3. Open your **Downloads** folder and double-click the `.msi` file.
4. Choose **Next**, read and accept the license if you agree, and keep the default installation folder and features, including **Add to PATH**. You do not need the optional extra tools for compiling native modules.
5. Choose **Install**, allow the installation if Windows asks, then choose **Finish**.
6. Open a **new** Command Prompt from the Start menu. Type `node --version` and press Enter. A result such as `v24.x.x` (with actual numbers in place of the x's) means installation succeeded. If the command is not recognized, restart Windows and try again.

#### macOS: install once

1. Open the download page above and select **macOS** and **LTS**.
2. Download the **macOS Installer (.pkg)**.
3. Open **Downloads** in Finder and double-click the `.pkg` file.
4. Choose **Continue**, read the license and choose **Agree** if you accept it, then choose **Install**. Keep the default location and enter your Mac password if requested.
5. Choose **Close** when installation finishes.
6. Open a **new** Terminal window using Spotlight (Command+Space, type `Terminal`, press Return). Type `node --version` and press Return. A version number means installation succeeded. If the command is not found, restart Terminal and check that the installer finished.

**Setup is complete when `node --version` prints a version number.** npm comes with the installer, but you do not need to run it. You do not need Python, Quarto, an editor extension, or another server application to play these games.

On Linux, use the Linux instructions on the same official Node.js download page, confirm `node --version`, and follow the terminal method below. The included double-click launchers are for Windows and macOS.

### Easiest way: double-click the Game Lab launcher

1. If the book arrived as a ZIP file, extract it first: on Windows, right-click it and choose **Extract All**; on macOS, double-click the ZIP.
2. Open the extracted `Quarto_Doc` folder. You should see `games`, `scripts`, and both `start-game-lab` launcher files together. Keep them together; do not move just the launcher or a single game out of this folder.
3. Start the launcher for your computer:

- On **macOS**, double-click `start-game-lab.command`.
- On **Windows**, double-click `start-game-lab.bat`.

The launcher starts the local server and opens the Game Lab in your usual browser at **[http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/](http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/)**. Choose **Collision Playground** and press an arrow key to check that it responds. Seeing the menu and a moving shape confirms the local setup works. Leave its window open while you play. To stop the server, close that window or press Ctrl+C in it.

If your computer asks for permission to run the launcher, do not ignore the warning. Ask an adult or teacher to check that the file came from this textbook folder. If school rules block launcher files, use the terminal method below.

### If setup does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `node` is not recognized / command not found | Close old terminal windows after installing Node.js; open a new one and check `node --version`. Restart the computer if needed. |
| Mac says the `.command` file cannot run or lacks permission | Use the terminal method below; it runs the same server without the launcher. |
| The launcher is blocked by school policy | Ask your teacher for an approved setup or hosted copy. |
| Browser does not open automatically | Leave the server window open and enter `http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/` in the browser's address bar. |
| Browser says it cannot connect | Start the launcher again and keep its window open. The local URL works only while the server is running on this computer. |
| Address begins with `file:///` or the game stays on “Loading” | Open the HTTP menu address above and choose the game there. |
| `EADDRINUSE` / port 8000 already in use | Use an already-running Game Lab window, or stop your earlier Game Lab with Ctrl+C and start it again. |
| 2D works, but a 3D game fails | Check internet access to `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, the visible game error, and WebGL2/hardware acceleration. Reinstalling Node.js will not fix a blocked CDN request. |

### Terminal method

On Windows, open the extracted `Quarto_Doc` folder in File Explorer, click its address bar, type `cmd`, and press Enter. A Command Prompt opens in that folder.

On macOS, open Terminal, type `cd` followed by a space, drag the extracted `Quarto_Doc` folder from Finder into Terminal, and press Return. This fills in the correct path even if it contains spaces.

You can also type the path yourself:

```bash
cd "/path/to/your/Quarto_Doc"
```

Replace `/path/to/your/Quarto_Doc` with the real location on your computer. Then run:

```bash
node scripts/serve.mjs
```

Leave that terminal window open while you play. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/` to choose a project. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/preview.html` to read the included HTML edition. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. The server listens only on your computer's loopback interface; it is a development tool, not a public hosting service.

No `npm install` is needed. If the terminal says that `node` is not recognized or not found, repeat the Node.js setup with an adult or teacher.

The browser's trip is simple: browser asks for `main.js` or an image, the local server finds that file in the textbook folder, and the browser receives it. Double-clicking an HTML file is not enough for these module-based projects because module, model, and JSON loading use browser requests. Another local static server also works, but keep the whole folder tree together.

## Choose a project

| Project | Chapter | Controls and purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collision Playground | 15–16 | Move with arrows/WASD or drag the player. Switch shape and turn wall blocking on or off. |
| Robot Orchard | 15–18 | Start; move with A/D or left/right; jump with Space/up/W; P pauses, R restarts, H shows hitboxes. Collect every gem and enter the portal. |
| Robot Island Explorer | 19–20 | Move with arrows/WASD; drag to orbit the camera; scroll to zoom. Collect four gems. Crates are decorative in this non-physics project. |
| Rapier Drop Lab | 21 | Drop again; orbit the camera; show colliders. Compare three bounce coefficients. |
| Marble Quest | 22 | Start; arrows/WASD move the marble; P pauses, R restarts, H shows colliders. Collect five gems and enter the gate. Falling costs a life. |
| 3D Asset Workshop | 20 | Change the robot body's color, orbit the view, and export your own GLB file. |

Click the game canvas before using keys. Movement controls are intentionally world-relative in the 3D games: W/up moves toward negative Z even if you rotate the exploration camera. The lab also supplies large onscreen controls where movement is needed. These are useful alternatives, not a claim that every canvas interaction is fully accessible to every player.

## Find the source you need

```text
chapters/               The textbook's Quarto chapters
figures/                Original diagrams with editable SVGs used by Chapters 15-22
games/
  index.html            Game Lab menu
  collision-lab/        Shape detection and wall-response experiment
  robot-orchard/        Complete 2D game and editable level.json
  three-explorer/       Three.js exploration without physics
  physics-lab/          Rapier bounce experiment
  marble-quest/         Complete 3D physics game
  asset-workshop/       GLB model customization and export
  shared/               Input, loops, collision helpers, styles, 3D setup
  assets/               Original SVG, PNG, GLB, JSON, and WAV files
scripts/                Local server, dependency download, book builders
start-game-lab.command  macOS double-click launcher
start-game-lab.bat      Windows double-click launcher
tests/                  Automated checks for reusable game logic
```

The complete project folders are the source of truth for runnable code. Snippets in the chapter explain selected pieces; some are deliberately simplified to focus on one idea. Do not append every snippet to `main.js` as though they were all additional instructions.

## Use the custom asset pack

The supplied robot sprite has four 64 by 64 frames. Edit the SVG source while keeping the 256 by 64 sheet size, or replace it with a PNG sprite sheet and update the image path. An image's transparent space is not a collider. Keep the player's physics dimensions separate from the drawing dimensions.

The 3D pack contains `robot.glb`, `crate.glb`, and `gem.glb`. `model-specifications.json` records their origins and dimensions. They are rigid models without a skeleton or animation clips. Move and rotate their roots in the game; use a different animated GLB only after adding animation handling.

The artwork and short collection sound were created for this project. The asset permission statement in `games/assets/ASSET_LICENSE.md` allows reuse and modification. It does not grant rights to unrelated images, commercial characters, or library code. When adding downloaded assets, record their source and license.

## Make the 3D projects available offline

By default, import maps load Three.js `0.180.0` and Rapier's compatibility package `0.17.3` from jsDelivr. These fixed versions keep the four 3D projects on the same dependency set. On a computer with internet access, Python 3 can download the two packages and switch the import maps to local copies:

```bash
python3 scripts/vendor-dependencies.py
```

On Windows, `py scripts/vendor-dependencies.py` may be the appropriate command. Keep `games/vendor/` with the project when copying it to another computer. Test every 3D page once while offline. Continue using the local server even after downloading the dependencies.

The script retains the packages' licenses. To switch the pages back to their original CDN imports, use `python3 scripts/vendor-dependencies.py --cdn`. Downloading packages and changing browser caches can be subject to your computer or network's restrictions.

## Debug in layers

::: {.callout-warning title="A blank page is not automatically a game-logic bug" icon="false"}
Check the page's visible error message and then the browser console. First check that the local server is running. Next check file paths and dependency requests. For a 3D page, check WebGL2 support and hardware acceleration. Only after the scene loads should you investigate collisions and score rules.
:::

| Symptom | Check first |
| --- | --- |
| A model or JSON file is not found | Keep the folder tree together; check spelling, capitalization, and the Network panel. |
| A 3D page reports a module error | Check internet/CDN access or run the optional dependency-download script. |
| The ball passes through the ground | Check that both relevant shapes have colliders, dimensions match, and the physics world is stepped. |
| The player stops far from a wall | Show hitboxes/colliders; compare the collision shape with the visible asset. |
| A score increases repeatedly | Collect only once and ignore end-of-overlap events. |
| Movement continues after changing tabs | Clear input state on blur and pause the game appropriately. |
| Restart makes the game faster | Look for a second animation loop or duplicated event listeners. |
| Sound is silent | Enable the sound option after starting; browser audio rules may require a user action. |

## Test before changing several things

From the project root, run:

```bash
node --test tests/*.test.mjs
```

These tests check reusable collision and game-rule functions. They do not replace playtesting, visual review, or running Rapier's actual simulation. After editing a rule, test its edge cases and then play the game. Make one change at a time so the result teaches you something.
